title: Chapter 96 — The Try-Works
paragraphs: Besides her hoisted boats, an American whaler is outwardly distinguished by her try-works. She presents the curious anomaly of the most solid masonry joined with oak and hemp to constitute the completed ship. It is as if a brick kiln were transported from an open field to her planks.

The try-works stand between the foremast and the mainmast, where the deck has the most room. The timbers underneath are specially strong, built to carry the weight of an almost solid block of brick and mortar about ten feet by eight and five feet high. The foundation does not go through the deck; instead, the masonry is bolted firmly to the surface by heavy iron knees that brace it on every side and screw it down to the timbers. Its sides are cased in wood, and its top is completely covered by a large, sloping, battened hatch. Take off this hatch and you uncover the great try-pots. There are two of them, and each holds several barrels. When they are not in use, they are kept remarkably clean. Sometimes they are polished with soapstone and sand until the insides shine like silver punch-bowls. On night watches some cynical old sailors will crawl into them and curl up there for a nap. While the pots are being polished — one man in each, side by side — plenty of confidential talk passes back and forth over the iron rims. It is also a place for deep mathematical thought. It was in the Pequod's left-hand try-pot, with the soapstone busily circling around me, that the remarkable fact first struck me, indirectly, that in geometry all bodies sliding along the cycloid, my soapstone for example, will descend from any point in exactly the same time.

Take the fire-board off the front of the try-works and you expose the bare masonry on that side, pierced by the two iron mouths of the furnaces, directly below the pots. These mouths have heavy iron doors. A shallow tank running under the whole enclosed base of the works keeps the fierce heat of the fire from passing into the deck. A funnel fitted at the back keeps this tank topped up with water as fast as it evaporates. There are no outside chimneys; the flues open straight out of the back wall. And here let us go back for a moment.
It was about nine o'clock at night that the Pequod's try-works were first fired up on this present voyage. It fell to Stubb to oversee the business.

"All ready there? Off hatch, then, and start her. You, cook, light the works." That was easy, since the carpenter had been stuffing his shavings into the furnace all through the voyage. It should be said here that on a whaling voyage the first fire in the try-works has to be fed with wood for a while. After that no wood is used, except to get the regular fuel burning quickly. The point is this: once it has been tried out, the crisp, shriveled blubber, now called scraps or fritters, still holds a good deal of its oil. These fritters feed the flames. Like a bloated, burning martyr, or a misanthrope consuming himself, the whale, once lit, supplies his own fuel and burns with his own body. If only he would consume his own smoke too! For his smoke is horrible to breathe, and breathe it you must; not only that, you must live in it for the time being. It has an unspeakable, wild, Hindu smell, the kind that may hang around funeral pyres. It smells like the left wing of the day of judgment; it is an argument for the pit.

By midnight the works were going full blast. We had cast off the carcass and set sail; the wind was rising, and the darkness over the wild ocean was intense. But the fierce flames licked that darkness up as they shot out in forks from the sooty flues every so often, lighting every high rope in the rigging as if with the famous Greek fire. The burning ship drove on, as though she had been sent without mercy on some errand of vengeance. In just this way the brigs of the bold Hydriote Canaris, loaded with pitch and sulfur, came out of their harbors at midnight with broad sheets of flame for sails, bore down on the Turkish frigates, and wrapped them in fire.

With the hatch lifted off the top of the works, there was now a wide hearth in front of them. On it stood the Tartarean shapes of the pagan harpooners, who are always the stokers on a whale-ship. With huge pronged poles they tossed hissing masses of blubber into the scalding pots or stirred up the fires underneath, until the flames shot out of the doors like curling snakes and snapped at their feet. The smoke rolled away in sullen heaps. Every time the ship pitched, the boiling oil pitched with her, as if it longed to leap into their faces. Across from the mouth of the works, on the far side of the wide wooden hearth, was the windlass, which served as a sea-going sofa. The watch lounged there when they had nothing else to do, staring into the red heat of the fire until their eyes felt scorched in their heads. Their tawny faces, now thick with grime from smoke and sweat, their matted beards, and by contrast the barbaric brilliance of their teeth were all strangely lit up by the flickering blaze of the works. As they told each other their unholy adventures, tales of terror in words of mirth; as their uncivilized laughter forked up out of them like the flames from the furnace; as the harpooners gestured wildly back and forth in front of them with their huge pronged forks and dippers; as the wind howled on, and the sea leaped, and the ship groaned and dove, and yet steadily drove her red hell farther and farther into the blackness of the sea and the night, and scornfully champed the white bone in her mouth, and spat viciously all around her; then the rushing Pequod, loaded with savages and freighted with fire, burning a corpse and plunging into that blackness of darkness, seemed the physical counterpart of her monomaniac commander's soul.

So it seemed to me as I stood at her helm, and for long hours silently guided the way of this fire-ship on the sea. Wrapped in darkness myself for that interval, I only the better saw the redness, the madness, the ghastliness of others. The continual sight of the fiendish shapes before me, capering half in smoke and half in fire, at last bred kindred visions in my soul, as soon as I began to yield to that unaccountable drowsiness that always came over me at a midnight helm.

But that night in particular something strange happened to me, something I have never been able to explain. I jerked awake from a brief sleep on my feet, horribly aware that something was fatally wrong. The jawbone tiller was hitting my side, where I had been leaning against it; in my ears was the low hum of sails just starting to shake in the wind. I thought my eyes were open, and I was half aware of putting my fingers to the lids and mechanically stretching them even wider. Yet in spite of all this I could see no compass in front of me to steer by, though it seemed only a minute since I had been watching the card in the light of the steady binnacle lamp. There seemed to be nothing ahead of me but a jet-black gloom, made ghastly now and then by flashes of red. My strongest impression was that whatever swift, rushing thing I was standing on was not so much heading for any harbor ahead as fleeing from every harbor behind. A stark, bewildered feeling, like death, came over me. My hands clutched the tiller convulsively, but with the crazy idea that the tiller had somehow, by some enchantment, been turned upside down. My God! What is the matter with me? I thought. And then I saw it: in my brief sleep I had turned around and was facing the ship's stern, with my back to her bow and the compass. In an instant I turned back, just in time to keep the vessel from flying up into the wind and very likely capsizing. How glad and how grateful I was to be free of this unnatural hallucination of the night, and of the fatal danger of being brought by the lee!

Do not look too long in the face of the fire, O man! Never dream with your hand on the helm! Do not turn your back to the compass; heed the first hint of the hitching tiller; do not believe the artificial fire when its redness makes all things look ghastly. Tomorrow, in the natural sun, the skies will be bright; those who glared like devils in the forking flames, the morning will show in far different, at least gentler, relief — the glorious, golden, glad sun, the only true lamp — all others but liars!

Nevertheless, the sun does not hide Virginia's Dismal Swamp, nor Rome's accursed Campagna, nor the wide Sahara, nor all the millions of miles of deserts and of griefs beneath the moon. The sun does not hide the ocean, which is the dark side of this earth, and which is two-thirds of this earth. So therefore, that mortal man who has more of joy than sorrow in him — that mortal man cannot be true — not true, or undeveloped. With books the same. The truest of all men was the Man of Sorrows, and the truest of all books is Solomon's, and Ecclesiastes is the fine hammered steel of woe. "All is vanity." ALL. This willful world has not yet grasped unchristian Solomon's wisdom. But he who dodges hospitals and jails and walks fast crossing graveyards and would rather talk of operas than hell — who calls Cowper, Young, Pascal, Rousseau poor devils, all of them sick men, and throughout a carefree lifetime swears by Rabelais as supremely wise and therefore jolly — not that man is fitted to sit down on tombstones and break the green damp mold with the unfathomably wondrous Solomon.

But even Solomon, he says, "the man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain" — that is, even while he is still alive — "in the congregation of the dead." So do not surrender yourself to fire, or it may turn you upside down and deaden you, as it did me for a time. There is a wisdom that is woe, but there is a woe that is madness. And in some souls there is a Catskill eagle that can dive down into the blackest gorges and just as well soar out of them again and vanish into the sunny spaces. And even if he flies forever inside the gorge, that gorge is in the mountains, so that even at the bottom of his lowest swoop the mountain eagle is still higher than other birds on the plain, even when they soar.
